import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 481

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/481](https://www.erdosproblems.com/481)
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980), p.96.
- [Kl82] Klarner, David A., *A sufficient condition for certain semigroups to be free*.
  J. Algebra (1982), 140-148.
- [KoTa22] Kolpakov, Alexander and Talambutsa, Alexey, *On free semigroups of affine maps on the
  real line*. Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. (2022), 2301-2307.
-/

namespace Erdos481

/--
For a finite sequence of $n$ (not necessarily distinct) integers $A = (x_1,\ldots,x_n)$, the
sequence `T a b A` of length $rn$ given by $(a_ix_j+b_i)_{1\leq j\leq n, 1\leq i\leq r}$.
-/
def T {r : ℕ} (a b : Fin r → ℕ) (A : List ℕ) : List ℕ :=
  (List.finRange r).flatMap (fun i : Fin r => A.map (fun x : ℕ => a i * x + b i))

/--
Let $a_1,\ldots,a_r,b_1,\ldots,b_r\in \mathbb{N}$ such that $\sum_{i}\frac{1}{a_i}>1$. For any
finite sequence of $n$ (not necessarily distinct) integers $A=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ let $T(A)$ denote
the sequence of length $rn$ given by
$$(a_ix_j+b_i)_{1\leq j\leq n, 1\leq i\leq r}.$$
Prove that, if $A_1=(1)$ and $A_{i+1}=T(A_i)$, then there must be some $A_k$ with repeated
elements.

This is true. This appears to have first been shown by Klarner [Kl82], with a generalisation
given by Kolpakov and Talambutsa [KoTa22]. Essentially the same proof was found independently by
Barreto in the comment section.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_481 {r : ℕ} (a b : Fin r → ℕ) (ha : ∀ i, 0 < a i)
    (hab : 1 < ∑ i, (1 : ℝ) / a i) :
    ∃ k, ¬ ((T a b)^[k] [1]).Nodup := by
  sorry

end Erdos481

reformulations.difference: The implementation uses natural-number lists and enumerates the affine-map index before the input-list index. The source describes integer sequences and writes the input index first.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Starting at [1], natural coefficients keep every reachable value in ℕ (indeed positive under ha). Casting to ℤ commutes with T and every iterate, and injectivity of the cast preserves and reflects Nodup. Interchanging the two loops enumerates exactly the same occurrences in a different order; the corresponding iterated lists are permutations, so the existence of a repeated element is unchanged. Both existential equivalences were proved in the scratch file.

reformulations.difference: Lean permits zero intercepts b_i, rather than requiring the positive-integer convention implicit in the source's assertion that the minimum grows at every step.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The universal positive-intercept and nonnegative-intercept versions are equivalent. If some generator is the identity, hab forces at least two indices, and the words ij and ji give a collision after two iterations. Otherwise set h(x)=2x−1 and b'_i=a_i−1+2b_i>0. On the positive orbit, h(a_i x+b_i)=a_i h(x)+b'_i; h fixes 1 and is injective. Thus the positive-intercept theorem transfers a collision to the original orbit, while the converse is specialization. This universal ↔ was proved in Lean without using the sorry theorem.

review.notes: Both declarations were checked. The source's PROVED (LEAN) status agrees with research solved; no answer slot or formal_proof record is present. Scratch checks establish the length r·length(A), the repeated-position interpretation of ¬Nodup, recurrence/indexing equivalence, positivity of reachable values, exclusion of r=0 and r=1 by hab, and satisfiable concrete examples. The original book's minimum-bound formulation is explicitly simplified by the current cited source. All scratch checks compile successfully. Klarner's full text remained publisher-blocked; its relevant result and attribution were checked through the cited Kolpakov–Talambutsa paper, which explicitly generalizes Theorem 1.1 and reproduces its argument.
